chunks: How brushes stay in contact. The question: How do brushes maintain contact with the commutator?
Brushes stay in contact with the commutator because springs push them against it. Each brush sits in a holder that lets it slide in and out.
As the brush wears shorter, the spring pushes it further forward, so contact stays firm. A flexible wire braid carries the current so the spring does not have to.
Think of a mechanical pencil. The lead sits in a sleeve, and as you write and it wears down, the lead is pushed forward so it always touches the paper.
A brush works the same way: the spring keeps feeding it toward the commutator as it shortens.
The analogy has one gap: a brush needs a controlled, fairly constant force, not just any push.
A spring-loaded brush in its holder.
The spring supplies the normal force F N ; the flexible pigtail (red) carries the current to the terminal so the spring and the sliding fit of the holder are not current paths.
The brush face rides on the commutator; the part of the brush below the dashed line is the length that will wear away, over which the spring must keep pushing it down.
Brush holder: a guide or box that lets the brush slide freely. Spring: the part that pushes the brush onto the commutator.
Pigtail: a flexible copper braid carrying current from the brush to the terminal. Contact force: how hard the brush presses. Too low causes bouncing and sparks.
Too high wears things fast. Commutator: the copper segments the brush rides on.
A new brush is 12 mm long and sits in its holder with a spring behind it. After a long time it wears down to 6 mm.
The spring has extended 6 mm further forward and is still pressing the brush against the commutator.
The current does not pass through the spring: it travels through the pigtail, so the spring stays cool and the brush moves freely.
That is the whole idea: a spring feeds the brush forward as it wears.
"Springs push the brushes onto the commutator.
Each brush slides in a holder box, and a spring behind it, a coil spring, a constant-force strip spring, or a torsion arm, keeps a set pressure, around 1. 5 to 2.
5 psi for carbon, as the brush wears down. A flexible copper pigtail carries the current so the spring doesn't. In small motors the brush is itself a springy metal finger.
Too little force means bounce and sparking, too much means fast wear and friction."
